claims.text: The starting FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating is susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading.
Creep resistance is governed by an interaction between lattice distortion and nanoscale precipitation hardening.
The interaction between lattice distortion and precipitation hardening inhibits dislocation motion.
The interaction between lattice distortion and precipitation hardening inhibits grain-boundary sliding.
Controlled thermal treatment can introduce nanoscale precipitates into the coating.
Thermally introduced nanoscale precipitates enhance precipitation hardening.
The nanoscale precipitates are distributed within the alloy matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Obstructing dislocation motion and stabilizing grain boundaries reduces creep deformation under sustained stress.
At identical stress and temperature, the precipitate-containing treated coating will have a significantly lower creep rate than the untreated coating.
The proposed creep-resistance mechanism operates only over temperatures at which the precipitates remain stable and effective obstacles to dislocation motion.
Variations in precipitate size, distribution, and thermal stability can alter the magnitude of the creep-rate reduction.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction in the treated coating under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
